4: Industrial machines, electrical panels, boilers and processing equipment can develop dangerous conditions such as overheating, gas leakage, excessive current or fire. If these conditions are not detected and acted upon quickly, they can damage equipment, stop production and endanger people. A microcontroller-based fault detection system continuously watches the plant through sensors, warns the operator when values start to drift, and shuts the equipment down safely when a limit is crossed. The proposed project, “LPC2148 Based Multi-Sensor Fault Detection System Using Interrupts, Timers and Safe Shutdown”, implements such a protection system using the LPC2148 ARM7 microcontroller.

The LPC2148 is a 32-bit ARM7TDMI-S microcontroller with 512 KB of flash memory, 40 KB of RAM and a maximum operating frequency of 60 MHz using its on-chip PLL. It integrates all the peripherals needed for this application: a 10-bit ADC for reading analog sensors, 32-bit timers for periodic scheduling, external interrupt inputs (EINT0–EINT3), a Vectored Interrupt Controller (VIC), a watchdog timer, UART serial ports and general-purpose I/O pins.

The system monitors five inputs. Three analog sensors measure quantities that change gradually: an LM35 temperature sensor, an MQ-2 gas/smoke sensor and an ACS712 current sensor, connected to ADC channels AD0.1–AD0.3. Two digital inputs represent events that need an instant response: a flame sensor on P0.3/EINT1 and an emergency-stop push button on P0.16/EINT0. The outputs are a load relay that powers the protected equipment, a buzzer, red/yellow/green status LEDs, a 16×2 LCD in 4-bit mode and a UART fault log.

The key design question is how to structure the software. The proposed design uses external interrupts for emergency events so that they are handled within microseconds, Timer0 interrupts every 100 ms to schedule periodic sensor checking without blocking delays, and a dedicated safe shutdown routine that always switches the load off first, raises the alarm and latches the fault until a manual reset. A three-state machine (NORMAL, WARNING, SHUTDOWN), a three-sample confirmation filter against false alarms and the on-chip watchdog timer complete the design.

The firmware is developed in Embedded C using Keil µVision. The generated HEX file is loaded into Proteus to verify the operation of the sensors, interrupts, relay, alarms and LCD before implementing the system on hardware. The system can be applied to motor protection, industrial safety panels, server-room monitoring, kitchen and boiler safety, and laboratory equipment protection.
5: The workflow of the proposed fault detection system consists of initialization, self-testing, continuous monitoring, fault classification, safe shutdown, alarm output and recovery. The system begins at the Start block when power is applied or the reset button is pressed. The very first action is to hold the load relay OFF, so that the protected equipment never runs before the system has confirmed that conditions are safe.

In the Initialization stage, the PLL is configured to raise the system clock from the 12 MHz crystal to 60 MHz. The GPIO pins for the relay, buzzer and LEDs are configured as outputs and the reset key as an input. The 16×2 LCD is initialized in 4-bit mode, UART0 is set to 9600 baud for the fault log, and pins P0.28–P0.30 are switched to their ADC function.

Next, the Self Test stage scans all sensors three times. Only if every reading is below its critical limit is the load relay switched ON and the green LED lit. The system then enables its interrupts: EINT0 and EINT1 are configured for falling-edge detection, Timer0 is started with a 100 ms period, all three sources are registered in the VIC, and the watchdog timer is started. The microcontroller now enters the Monitoring stage, where the main loop waits for flags set by interrupts.

Events that cannot wait are handled through external interrupts. Pressing the emergency-stop button produces a falling edge on P0.16/EINT0, and a flame detection pulls P0.3/EINT1 low. The VIC immediately transfers control to EINT0_ISR or EINT1_ISR. Emergency stop is given VIC slot 0 (highest priority), flame slot 1 and Timer0 slot 2. Each of these ISRs simply calls safe_shutdown(), clears its EXTINT flag and writes VICVectAddr = 0. Because they do very little work, they finish in microseconds and the response does not depend on what the main loop was doing.
6: Temperature, gas and current change slowly and reading the ADC takes time, so these sensors are checked periodically rather than inside an interrupt. Timer0 is programmed with a prescaler of 59 (1 MHz count) and a match value of 100000, so it interrupts every 100 ms. TIMER0_ISR only sets the flag check_due. The main loop sees the flag and calls scan_sensors(), which reads the three ADC channels and compares each value with its warning and critical limits. A reading must stay above the critical limit for three consecutive scans (300 ms) before it is treated as a real fault; this filters out noise spikes. If any value is above its warning limit, the system enters the WARNING state, and the Timer0 ISR blinks the yellow LED and beeps the buzzer.

Every critical fault, whether detected by an interrupt or by the periodic scan, goes through one function, safe_shutdown(). It first de-energizes the load relay to remove the hazard, then switches on the red LED and continuous buzzer, latches the first fault cause in fault_code and sets log_due so that the main loop sends the fault record over UART. The relay is wired so that the load runs only while the coil is energized; therefore a power failure or a CPU reset also switches the load off. The shutdown is latched: the system restarts only when the reset key is pressed and a fresh sensor scan confirms that all values are back to normal. The watchdog timer, fed once in every main-loop pass, resets the microcontroller if the software ever hangs, which also releases the relay.

In the Output stage, the LCD shows the live temperature and gas readings together with NORMAL, WARNING or the fault name, and the LEDs and buzzer give a visual and audible indication. Finally, the system feeds the watchdog and returns to monitoring. The process repeats continuously for as long as the system is powered.

Thus, the complete workflow can be summarized as: Power ON/Reset → Load OFF → Initialization → Self Test → Enable Interrupts & Watchdog → Monitor → Timer0 Tick → Sensor Scan → Classify (Normal / Warning / Critical) → E-Stop/Flame Interrupt → Safe Shutdown → Alarm & LCD & UART Log → Reset & Re-check → Repeat Continuously.
7: The implementation of the LPC2148-based fault detection system is carried out using Keil µVision for program development and compilation, and Proteus for simulation. The complete implementation involves creating the project, selecting the microcontroller, adding the source program, configuring the target, compiling, generating the HEX file and finally simulating the circuit.

Open the installed Keil µVision 5 (MDK-ARM) development environment. The MDK-ARM version is used because the LPC2148 is an ARM7-based microcontroller. Select Project → New µVision Project, give a suitable name such as LPC2148_Fault_Detection and choose a separate folder for the project files.

After the project is saved, Keil opens the Select Device for Target window. Selecting the correct device is important because Keil uses this information to configure the registers, memory areas, startup files and compiler settings.

Search for LPC2148 and select it under NXP → LPC2000 → LPC2100 Series, then click OK. When Keil asks whether to add the startup file (Startup.s) to the project, select Yes; it sets up the stacks and the interrupt vector table used by the VIC.

Right-click Source Group 1, choose Add New Item to Group, select C File (.c) and save it as main.c. This file holds the complete program for ADC sensor reading, Timer0 and external interrupt handling, LCD and UART output, and safe shutdown.

Write the program inside main.c, including the LPC214x.h header to access the LPC2148 registers. The program configures the PLL, GPIO directions, LCD, UART0 and ADC; defines EINT0_ISR, EINT1_ISR and TIMER0_ISR using the __irq keyword; and implements scan_sensors(), safe_shutdown(), the state machine and the watchdog routines. Save the file using Ctrl + S.
Open Options for Target and enter the crystal frequency as 12.000 MHz in the Target tab. The firmware configures the PLL itself, so the CPU and peripheral clock run at 60 MHz.

Compile the project using Build Target or F7. The Build Output window shows the compilation status, program size, errors and warnings. A successful build should report 0 errors; any warnings should be checked.
Open Options for Target → Output, enable Create HEX File and click OK. Rebuild the project so that Keil generates the .hex file required by the Proteus LPC2148 model.

22: The block diagram represents the complete hardware architecture of the fault detection system, with the LPC2148 ARM7TDMI-S microcontroller as the central control unit. The sensor input section contains the LM35, MQ-2 and ACS712 connected to ADC channels AD0.1–AD0.3, and the flame sensor and emergency-stop button connected to the external interrupt pins EINT1 and EINT0. The 5 V sensor modules are connected through resistor dividers so that the ADC input never exceeds 3.3 V.

The output section contains the relay driver (2N2222 transistor with a 1N4007 flyback diode) controlling the load relay through P0.15, the buzzer, the three status LEDs, the 16×2 LCD in 4-bit mode on P1.16–P1.21 and the UART link to a PC. The clock circuit (12 MHz crystal with PLL) and the reset circuit provide timing and initialization. Signals flow from the sensors into the controller, which processes them and drives the alarm and switching outputs.
23: The firmware is divided into four layers. The interrupt layer contains short ISRs that only react or set flags. The application layer is the main super-loop, which performs the sensor scan, runs the state machine, updates the LCD and UART and feeds the watchdog. The safety layer contains safe_shutdown() and the watchdog timer, and the driver layer contains the low-level routines for the ADC, LCD, UART, timers and interrupts. Shared variables between ISRs and the main loop are declared volatile.
24: When the emergency-stop button is pressed or a flame is detected, a falling edge is generated on EINT0 or EINT1. The VIC identifies the source and transfers control to the corresponding ISR, which calls safe_shutdown(), clears the interrupt flag and returns. Timer0 generates an interrupt every 100 ms; its ISR sets the check_due and disp_due flags that the main program uses to schedule sensor scanning and display updates. After every ISR, control returns to the main program.
Event (E-Stop / Flame / Timer0) → VIC (priority) → ISR → Safe Shutdown or Set Flag → Clear Flag → Return to Main Program → Scan / Log / Display → Repeat
25: The system is always in one of three states. In NORMAL the load runs with the green LED on. In WARNING the load continues to run while the yellow LED blinks and the buzzer beeps. In SHUTDOWN the load is switched off with the red LED and continuous buzzer; this state is latched and is left only when the reset key is pressed and the re-scan confirms healthy conditions.
27: The LPC2148-based multi-sensor fault detection system was designed to demonstrate how an ARM7 microcontroller can protect equipment by monitoring several sensors, raising alarms and shutting the system down safely when an abnormal condition occurs. The LPC2148 coordinates the temperature, gas, current and flame sensors, the emergency-stop input, the load relay, the alarm outputs, the LCD and the UART log.

The project answers the software-structure question through a clear division of responsibilities. External interrupts EINT0 and EINT1, given the highest VIC priorities, handle the emergency stop and flame detection instantly. Timer0 generates a 100 ms periodic interrupt that schedules sensor scanning, while the actual ADC reading and decision-making are done in the main loop so that the ISRs remain short. A three-sample confirmation filter prevents false alarms, and the NORMAL–WARNING–SHUTDOWN state machine separates early warnings from critical faults.

Safe shutdown is guaranteed through a single safe_shutdown() routine that switches the load off first, raises the alarm and latches the fault cause. Fail-safe relay wiring, a safe state at power-up, a power-on self test, a controlled manual reset with re-checking of all sensors, and the watchdog timer together ensure that the system always fails into a safe condition, even if the software hangs or power is lost.

The 16×2 LCD and the UART fault log give the operator clear information about the live sensor readings and the cause of any shutdown. The program was written and compiled in Keil µVision and converted into a HEX file for simulation in Proteus, allowing the complete behaviour to be verified before building the hardware.

The project provided practical experience in PLL clock configuration, ADC programming, timer and external interrupt handling through the VIC, GPIO interfacing, LCD and UART communication, and safety-oriented embedded software design. It can be extended by storing fault history in EEPROM, sending SMS alerts through a GSM module, adding more sensors such as vibration or voltage monitors, or connecting the system to an IoT dashboard for remote monitoring.

In conclusion, the proposed system successfully demonstrates how a microcontroller can detect abnormal conditions using interrupts and timer-based periodic checking, respond with alarms, and bring the system to a safe shutdown, forming a practical foundation for industrial safety and condition-monitoring applications.
